whyThisMatters: A lot of what feels true about packages, PR comments, and CI alerts is only partly right — and developers are targeted precisely because so much of the job runs on trusting routine signals quickly. A few minutes here will clear up what really matters when a dependency, a comment, or an outreach message already looks normal.
rememberThis: This month's reminder: familiar packaging is not proof. A plausible package name, a real-looking reviewer handle, or a CI alert styled like your own system can all be faked — check the actual source and domain every time, no matter how routine the request looks.

discussionPrompts: Ask how the team currently decides whether a new dependency is safe to add — is there an actual check, or does familiarity with the name do the deciding?
For the CI/CD myth, ask if anyone can name the team's real process for a deployment-credential problem — is emailing credentials ever really part of it?
Ask if anyone has run a setup script from an unsolicited recruiter or contributor message. What would make them pause next time?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get the dependency myth wrong. A plausible package name feels like enough of a check, so many people say it's fine to add without looking further. But attackers publish typosquatted or freshly-popular-looking packages specifically to pass that quick glance — the real check is publish history and maintainer reputation, not the name alone.

items.myth: A plausible package name and a reasonable download count mean it's safe to add as a dependency.
items.fact: Attackers publish typosquatted or freshly-popular-looking packages specifically to pass a quick glance. The real check is the maintainer's history, how long the package has existed, and whether an established alternative already does the job.
items.detail: A new package proposed under time pressure — "this fixes it faster, can we merge today" — is exactly when to slow down and check the package itself, not just the code in the PR that calls it.

items.myth: A comment from what looks like a real reviewer's account on my PR is always legitimate.
items.fact: A handle can be a near-identical typosquat, or a real account can be compromised. A login or re-authentication link inside a PR comment is never legitimate, regardless of whose name is attached to it.
items.detail: Check the CI or GitHub dashboard directly yourself instead of clicking a link in a comment — and look closely at the commenter's exact handle, not just how familiar it looks at a glance.

items.myth: If the code in a PR looks fine when you read the diff, it's safe to merge, dependency and all.
items.fact: A dependency's own install-time or import-time behaviour is not visible in the PR's diff. The package itself needs its own check — publish history and maintainer reputation — separate from reviewing the code that calls it.
items.detail: Reading the calling code carefully is good practice, but it tells you nothing about what a newly-added package actually does when it is installed or imported.

items.myth: An unsolicited recruiter message with a private repo and a coding challenge is a normal, harmless part of job hunting.
items.fact: This is a known way to deliver malware directly to developers, who are used to cloning repos and running setup scripts without much thought. Verify the recruiter and company independently before doing either.
items.detail: If you do proceed, open the challenge in an isolated environment rather than running the setup script on your main machine — the same caution you'd use for any code from a source you can't yet vouch for.

items.myth: CI/CD systems sometimes legitimately ask you to re-enter your Git username and access token by email if there's a build problem.
items.fact: Your real CI system authenticates you through the session you already have. It never asks you to retype your credentials in response to an alert email, no matter what reason is given.
items.detail: Any email asking you to "re-authorize" or "re-enter" deployment credentials should be treated as phishing — verify by opening the CI dashboard yourself, never through the email's link.

items.myth: Only production credentials are worth protecting — dev and test tokens are low risk.
items.fact: Dev and test tokens often reach the same pipelines and repositories as production ones, and are frequently reused or left unrotated for longer, making them just as valuable a target.
items.detail: Treat any CI, package-registry, or Git access token the same way regardless of which environment it's labelled for — a leaked "low risk" token is still a way into your systems.

items.myth: If an update notice for an approved AI coding extension says the marketplace is delayed, it's fine to install from the link it provides instead.
items.fact: A genuine extension update is never blocked from reaching its own marketplace listing. Any reason given to install outside the marketplace "just this once" is the actual signal to stop, not a reasonable workaround.
items.detail: Always check the official marketplace listing directly for an update yourself, rather than a link that claims to bypass it.

items.myth: Replying to a DevOps email with your service's current .env values is fine during a migration, since it saves everyone time.
items.fact: A genuine vault migration only ever asks you to act inside the vault UI yourself. Being asked to send secrets in cleartext by email, for any reason, is the actual signal to stop, regardless of the deadline attached.
items.detail: Rotate secrets yourself through the vault UI, and confirm any migration request with DevOps through a known channel before doing anything else.
